html:
The worst famine of Tokugawa Japan, from 1782 to 1788, named after the Tenmei era. It struck the northeast, the Tōhoku region, hardest.

Cold, wet summers ruined rice harvests several years running. In 1783 the volcano Mount Asama erupted in central Japan, spreading ash over farmland. The same year Iceland's Laki eruption cooled the northern hemisphere, which may have made matters worse. Many domains had shipped their rice south to sell in Osaka and Edo, leaving little in store.

Hundreds of thousands are thought to have died of hunger and disease, and whole villages emptied. Rice riots broke out in Edo and Osaka in 1787. The famine discredited the chief minister Tanuma Okitsugu, whose market minded policies were blamed. His successor Matsudaira Sadanobu launched the Kansei reforms, with grain stores, frugality laws and a return to stricter Confucian rule.
sum: The worst famine of Tokugawa Japan, from 1782 to 1788, named after the Tenmei era. It struck the northeast, the Tōhoku region, hardest.
